prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active forms, which made possible incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: B036 remains the strongest case before us, and round 1 did not weaken it: no one questioned its maturity, and every member grounded it in the same content. Proglucagon processing, the identification of the biologically active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, human incretin physiology and the mechanisms of action in pancreas, brain and gut lead to drugs whose benefit is confirmed independently in large randomized trials of diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. I hold the position I took in round 1 and move no further: a single prize part for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. I started from Knudsen in my opening and gave that up after reading colleagues, and nothing in the second round brings me back. The chair asked what criterion should settle the third slot. My answer is that the three-name limit should first protect the discovery of what the hormone is and does, because the engineered analogues have no target without it. The citation carries the therapeutic consequence in its wording. I also see no reason to add a second part. A single coherent story split into a discovery part and a drug part is less clean than one part, and none of B006, B042, B031 or B047 has an allocation that is clearly better resolved than this one.
statement.case_against: The attribution is imperfect and I do not think the record should pretend otherwise. Habener is outside the credited names and has a real claim to the early proglucagon and peptide work. Mojsov's priority on the active peptide is described as contested by every member, and none of us, myself included, has checked it against the supplied evidence. Knudsen's engineering of liraglutide and semaglutide is decisive for what patients receive, so a committee that values transformation of care as much as discovery could fairly regard this configuration as drawing the line in the wrong place. If the Committee concludes that Mojsov's contribution cannot be supported from the evidence in the file, I would accept the Knudsen version rather than leave the third slot to a name that cannot be defended. That is the one condition under which I would change, and I have not yet seen evidence that meets it.

responses.point: The chair argued that dropping Mojsov for Knudsen turns a discovery prize into a development prize and leaves the physiology with two people, but said he would move to Knudsen if her priority claim cannot be supported from the file.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of your argument and with its conditional. I would apply the condition narrowly. A contested allocation among discoverers is a weaker reason to drop someone than a showing that the contribution was not made. Nothing in the supplied material says the identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) form was not hers, and several of us say we have not verified it either way. So I read the uncertainty as a reason to word the citation around the physiology and the active peptides rather than around a single priority claim, not as a reason to switch. I would also not let our shared lack of verification count as evidence against her.

responses.point: Sandberg said Habener's absence is a real weakness and not just a caveat, that it weakens the Mojsov slot, and that the Knudsen option should be revisited if peptide-identification credit cannot be assigned fairly.
responses.response: This is the strongest challenge to my position, and it was my own opening view that you are now qualifying. Habener's absence does limit how completely the early peptide work can be rewarded. But it limits the Knudsen version equally, since replacing Mojsov with Knudsen does not put Habener back and instead thins the discovery side further. The absence is a constraint on the set of names we were given, not a point in favour of either third name. I would record it openly in the deliberation and keep the citation on the physiology of GLP-1 and its active forms, so that it does not assert an exclusive priority. On that footing I think the trio remains the best available allocation.

responses.point: El-Manira argued that if the earlier discoveries sit outside the credited names, a trio rewards development rather than discovery, and that applying the principle to B026 but not to B036 would be inconsistent. He said he could support Knudsen if the Committee explicitly argued for a therapeutic framing.
responses.response: I accept the consistency test, and it answers one of the chair's questions. Applied to B036 it works in our favour, because here the physiology and active peptide are carried by named laureates and only one early contributor is missing. For B026 and B031 the foundational discovery is largely outside the credited names, so the same test counts against them. I would not make the argument for the therapeutic framing myself. I made it in my opening and I now find it less persuasive than yours. That is why I do not expect to move back to Knudsen unless the Mojsov evidence fails.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius said a single GLP-1 prize with the physiology trio is cleaner than splitting one coherent story into a discovery part and a drug part, and that she regards Mojsov over Knudsen as close.
responses.response: I agree that one part is cleaner, and I would add the three-person limit as a practical reason. A second part would force a discovery part and a drug part to share the same three places, or would need a second achievement that adds more names. B031 is the strongest of the second-part options because it has two clean names, but you and I both note that its cloning and antibody-engineering foundations are outside the credited pair. I share your view that the Mojsov versus Knudsen choice is close, and I would not describe the trio as settled attribution. I only think it is the better of two imperfect options.

responses.point: Perlmann said B006 with Mori and Walter cannot be combined with GLP-1 under the three-person limit, and that he could move to a Knudsen configuration if colleagues show Mojsov's contribution is weaker than he recalls.
responses.response: The limit is a real constraint and I agree with your arithmetic. A GLP-1 trio plus Mori and Walter would mean five people, so B006 can only work as an alternative or as a replacement if GLP-1 stalls. That is why I keep it as an alternative and not as a second part. On Mojsov, I have not seen anyone present evidence that her contribution is weaker than we recall, only that it is disputed. Until someone does, I do not think the dispute alone should decide the slot.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority on the active GLP-1 peptide can be supported from the supplied evidence; this is the single point that would move me to Knudsen.
Whether the Committee reads the prize as the discovery of GLP-1 physiology or as the therapeutic arc, which decides the third name.
Whether Habener's absence from the credited names is recorded in the citation wording or only in the deliberation record, and whether it makes any allocation within three names unfair.
Whether the unfolded protein response, with a clean pair of names but indirect clinical impact, should replace B036 if the GLP-1 allocation stalls, or only stand as an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. My documented co-authors, including Castelo-Branco, Betsholtz, Ernfors, Frisen, Lundeberg, Kharchenko and Sandberg, are not credited names on any shortlisted ballot. Round 1 disclosures by colleagues of collaborations unrelated to credited names change nothing for me. Shared Karolinska Institutet affiliation is not treated as a conflict.
